write.desc: This topic defines the limit of a function f: A -> R at a limit point of its domain, trains the learner to prove and disprove limits from the epsilon-delta definition, and uses the sequential criterion as the bridge that brings the limit laws, order, squeeze and divergence tests over from sequences, ending with the one-sided, at-infinity and infinite variants of the definition.

points.name: The epsilon-delta definition of a functional limit
points.what: State lim_{x->c} f(x) = L for f: A -> R with 0 < |x - c| < delta and x in A, and explain why c must be a limit point of A (otherwise every L would qualify and the limit would not be unique) and why the value f(c), or whether f is even defined at c, plays no role.
outside: limit point (accumulation point) of a subset of R
reading and ordering nested quantifiers (for all epsilon there exists delta)
absolute value inequalities and the triangle inequality

points.name: Proving a limit from the definition: scratch work then proof
points.what: Find a delta by working backwards from |f(x) - L| < epsilon (scratch work) and then write the forward proof cleanly, for linear functions and for x^2, using a preliminary bound such as delta <= 1 and delta = min(1, ...) to control the extra factor.

points.name: How delta depends on epsilon and the point
points.what: Prove limits such as 1/x at c > 0 and sqrt x at c > 0 (and sqrt x at 0 from the right side of the domain), and see from the formulas for delta that it must shrink as c approaches a trouble spot, not only as epsilon shrinks.

points.name: Negating the limit definition
points.what: Write out 'f(x) does not tend to L as x -> c' (there is an epsilon such that every delta has some x in A with 0 < |x - c| < delta and |f(x) - L| >= epsilon) and 'the limit does not exist', and use it to show directly that a given L is not the limit.

points.name: The sequential criterion for functional limits
points.what: Prove that lim_{x->c} f(x) = L if and only if f(x_n) -> L for every sequence (x_n) in A with x_n != c and x_n -> c, the converse by contrapositive choosing x_n within delta = 1/n.
outside: definition of convergence of a sequence (epsilon-N)

points.name: Uniqueness and the algebraic limit laws for functions
points.what: Use the sequential criterion to prove that a functional limit is unique and that limits of sums, scalar multiples, products and quotients (with nonzero limit in the denominator) behave as expected, without redoing any epsilon-delta work.
outside: algebraic limit theorem for sequences (sums, products, quotients)

points.name: Order and squeeze for functional limits
points.what: Use the sequential criterion to prove that limits preserve non-strict inequalities between functions near c and the squeeze theorem for functions, and apply it to examples such as x sin(1/x) -> 0 as x -> 0.

points.name: Proving a limit does not exist with two sequences
points.what: Show that a limit fails to exist by finding sequences x_n -> c and y_n -> c (avoiding c) with f(x_n) and f(y_n) converging to different values or with f(x_n) divergent, as for sin(1/x) at 0 and the sign function at 0.

points.name: One-sided limits
points.what: Define the right-hand and left-hand limits at c (limits of the restriction of f to A intersected with (c, infinity) or (-infinity, c)), and prove that the two-sided limit exists and equals L exactly when both one-sided limits exist and equal L.

points.name: Limits at infinity
points.what: Define lim_{x->infinity} f(x) = L (for every epsilon there is M such that x > M in A gives |f(x) - L| < epsilon), write its negation, prove examples such as 1/x and (2x+1)/(x+3), and note that the sequential criterion and limit laws carry over.

points.name: Infinite limits
points.what: Define lim_{x->c} f(x) = infinity (for every M there is delta with f(x) > M whenever 0 < |x - c| < delta) and the variants as x -> infinity, write their negations, and prove examples such as 1/x^2 -> infinity at 0 and 1/x having no infinite two-sided limit at 0.
